A.explanation: About $400\text{ J}$ is a factor of 10 too small, corresponding to too low a mass or speed estimate.

B.explanation: With $m \approx 80\text{ kg}$ and $v \approx 10\text{ m s}^{-1}$, $\frac{1}{2}mv^2 \approx 4000\text{ J}$.

C.explanation: About $40\,000\text{ J}$ is a factor of 10 too large, as if $v$ was not halved or $v^2$ was about $1000$.

D.explanation: About $400\,000\text{ J}$ is a factor of 100 too large, far beyond human running speed and mass.

hints: Estimate the maximum running speed from the 100 m distance and an Olympic time of about $10\text{ s}$, giving $v$ near $10\text{ m s}^{-1}$.
Recall kinetic energy $E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$ and estimate the athlete mass as about $70$ to $80\text{ kg}$.
Calculate $\frac{1}{2} \times 80 \times 10^2$ and check which power of ten - $400$, $4000$, $40\,000$ or $400\,000\text{ J}$ - it is closest to.
walkthrough: Identify that no mass or speed is given, so both must be estimated for an Olympic 100 m sprinter.
Estimate mass $m \approx 70$ to $80\text{ kg}$ for an adult athlete.
Estimate maximum speed from $v \approx$ distance / time: $100\text{ m}$ in about $10\text{ s}$ gives $v \approx 10\text{ m s}^{-1}$.
Substitute estimates with units: $E_k \approx 0.5 \times 80\text{ kg} \times (10\text{ m s}^{-1})^2 = 0.5 \times 80 \times 100$.
Evaluate to $E_k \approx 4000\text{ J}$, with unit $\text{J} = \text{kg m}^2\text{ s}^{-2}$, correct to order of magnitude.
This is option B, while the other options are each a factor of 10 or more away.
